title: My First Week Teaching from a Script
author: SoL in the Wild
summary: A seventh-grade World Studies teacher reports on five days of teaching from word-for-word scripts, generated with Claude for Teachers and then heavily edited by hand, including several think-alouds and an Engelmann-style Direct Instruction lesson. He frames the experiment with a question he applies to any method: what problems is it likely to solve and what problems is it likely to create. On the benefit side, scripts made his explanations more concise, kept guided practice brisk, freed working memory so he could watch students more closely during independent practice, and forced him to make expert thinking visible. On the cost side, the delivery lost some emphasis and energy, and no script can anticipate every student response. He argues scripts can relieve working memory on overloaded days, that teachers and PLC teams should build and vet their own AI-assisted scripts when publishers fall short, and that scripting should be matched to the learning objective. He is candid that five days is a small sample and that planning time, not the script, may explain some gains.
points: Scripts shortened explanations and sped up guided practice because the examples, questions and scaffolds were decided in advance.
Knowing the questions and likely misconceptions ahead of time freed working memory for observing student work during independent practice.
Writing a think-aloud script forced hidden expert decisions into the open, which supports cognitive apprenticeship.
The trade-off is lost spontaneity and vocal emphasis, and no script replaces professional judgment about unplanned student responses.
He recommends team-based, human-vetted AI-assisted scripts matched to where students sit on the instructional hierarchy, not scripting every lesson.
quotes: I find that starting with those questions produces a much more useful conversation than simply asking whether I like an instructional approach or whether it aligns with my preferences. Every instructional decision comes with trade-offs.

Having a script helped me recognize those moments proactively before I was standing in front of students. I had already made decisions about what to explain, what examples to use, and what details to leave out.
Because I already knew the questions I was going to ask and the likely misconceptions I might encounter, I didn’t have to devote as much working memory to determining my responses.

Of course, no script can anticipate every student response or misconception. Students will always say or do things that you didn’t plan for, and responding to those moments requires professional teacher judgment and experience.

A script can clearly organize what a teacher says, but it cannot automatically reproduce the inflection, emphasis, personality, and energy that make an explanation effective. Those things still require deliberate delivery.

I found the availability of a script remarkably comforting and reassuring. There are days when I need to remember that we are all human and that relying on a prepared script will lead to clearer, more concise instruction rather than trying to reconstruct everything from memory.

I think a more sustainable path forward is for teachers, and preferably teams within schools and districts, to use AI to help develop scripts using the curriculum they’re already teaching aligned with the principles of effective explicit instruction and Direct Instruction.
My biggest takeaway from this experiment is that scripting, like all parts of good instruction, has to be matched to the instructional task and the learning objective.
context: He judges instructional methods by the problems they solve and the ones they create.
Pre-decided details let him resist seductive tangents that pull attention from core knowledge.
Offloading recall to the script left attention free for noticing student errors.
Scripts cannot cover the unexpected, so teacher judgment remains central.
Delivery, emphasis and energy still have to be practiced because the page does not carry them.
A script can ease working-memory overload on chaotic days without undermining professionalism.
AI-drafted scripts need human vetting, ideally by collaborative teams.
The right amount of scripting depends on what students are learning at that point.
